desc:
A positive integer is happy if repeatedly replacing it with the sum of the squares of its decimal digits eventually reaches 1. For example 19 -> 82 -> 68 -> 100 -> 1 is happy, while 2 -> 4 -> 16 -> 37 -> 58 -> 89 -> 145 -> 42 -> 20 -> 4 falls into a cycle that never contains 1.

Return how many integers in the range 1..n are happy.

Example: the happy numbers up to 10 are 1, 7, 10, so n = 10 gives 3; there are 20 happy numbers up to 100.
hints: Testing every number on its own with a cycle check is correct, but you repeat the same work over and over.
After one step every number up to 200,000 becomes at most 6 * 81 = 486, so only a few hundred values are ever 'reached'.

Decide happiness once for all values 1..486 (slow/fast pointers or a visited set), then for each x only compute the digit square sum and look the verdict up. The digit square sum of x can be derived from the one of x // 10.
editorial: A number is happy exactly when its digit-square-sum is happy (and 1 is happy), so the verdict for x depends only on s(x), the sum of squared digits. For x ≤ 200,000 we have s(x) ≤ 6 * 81 = 486.

Precompute happy[v] for v = 1..486 by running the fast/slow pointer test (advance slow by one application of s and fast by two; if fast lands on 1 the value is happy, if the pointers meet first it is not). Then compute s(x) for all x in order using s(x) = s(x // 10) + (x % 10)2 and count the x with happy[s(x)]. Total time O(n), memory O(n) for the s table (or O(1) if you recompute digits).
